title: Lent, forty days
hook: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter

segments.voice: Yesterday: the works of mercy, and the king who said I was hungry. Which work did you choose? Day two hundred sixty-six, the last day of our visit to the Catholic tradition.

One Wednesday in late winter, you might notice something odd on the train. A smudge of gray on someone's forehead. Then another, and another: a nurse, a guy in a suit, a teenager with earbuds. It isn't dirt. It's ash, put there that morning in the shape of a cross, with a few words that stop most people cold: remember that you are dust. It's the first day of a season that runs forty days, and it asks people to give something up. Today, to end our week with the Catholic tradition: Lent.
screen: `A GRAY SMUDGE ON THE TRAIN.` → `REMEMBER THAT YOU ARE DUST.` → `FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: The ashes come from Genesis, from God's words to Adam, in the King James Version: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." It sounds grim, but many Catholics find it freeing: you're not in charge of everything, and the time you have is a gift. Why forty? Because forty keeps turning up in the Bible as a time of testing and preparation: forty days of rain for Noah, forty years for Israel in the wilderness, forty days for Moses on the mountain. Above all, Jesus fasted forty days in the desert before he began to teach. Lent follows him there. It's a season of three practices, all from Jesus' teaching in Matthew six: prayer, fasting and almsgiving, which means giving to the poor. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and many go without meat on Fridays. Most also choose a personal sacrifice, sweets, social media, a daily coffee, or add something good instead. If you count the days from Ash Wednesday to Easter, you get more than forty; in the Western count, Sundays aren't counted, because every Sunday is a small Easter. Orthodox Christians keep their own Great Lent, starting on a Monday. The word Lent is plain old English for spring, from the lengthening days. Now look back at our week. The Eucharist: real presence. The rosary: one bead at a time. The saints: a cloud of witnesses. Sacred reading: read slowly. The Hail Mary: full of grace. The works of mercy: I was hungry. And Lent: forty days, walking toward Easter.
screen: `FOR DUST THOU ART.` · `FORTY: TESTING AND PREPARING.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `LENT — THE LENGTHENING DAYS.` · then, large: `FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give up one small thing for a day. Sit, and look honestly at your day. What do you reach for without thinking? The phone at red lights. A second dessert. A sharp comment. Choose one, just for today. Picture the moment you'll want it, and what you'll do with that gap instead: a breath, a prayer if you pray, a coin for someone. The bell holds the time.
Lent. From the old English word for spring: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving on the way to Easter. Today's word.
Your line: forty days. Today, keep your one small fast, and when the gap opens, fill it with something good. Day two hundred sixty-six. Tomorrow we visit Islam.

howItsDone: Catholics begin Lent with ashes on Ash Wednesday, fast that day and on Good Friday, abstain from meat on Fridays, and take on personal practices of prayer, fasting and almsgiving until Easter.
